title: The text itself
hook: scholars also test whether the text fits the Qur'an and known sunnah

segments.voice: Yesterday: the isnad, the chain of who told whom, link by link, back to the Prophet.

Aisha has just heard a report that troubles her. It came through people she respects: Umar, and his son Abdullah. It says a dead person is punished because their family weeps over them. Someone in the grave, punished for a grieving mother's tears? Aisha doesn't attack the men who carried it. She goes to the words themselves, and to the Qur'an. You've met this scene before, with Aisha the scholar. Today, look at what it shows: a hadith's text being weighed, not just its chain. Today, the matn.
screen: `A REPORT THAT TROUBLES HER.` → `NOT THE MEN, THE WORDS.` → `WEIGHED AGAINST THE QUR'AN.`

segments.voice: Matn is the text of a hadith, the part after the names: what was actually said or done. The chain asks who carried it. The matn asks: does this fit? Aisha's test, in Bukhari, is, in effect: may Allah have mercy on Umar, but the Prophet ﷺ didn't say that about a believer. He said it about a man who rejected faith, whose punishment was being increased while his family wept. Then she reaches for the Qur'an: enough for you is the Book, which says no soul carries another's load. In the version in Sahih Muslim she adds something gentle. The men who reported it weren't liars, she says. But hearing can slip. That's the whole idea in one breath: an honest chain can still carry a misheard sentence, so the words get tested on their own. Later scholars didn't simply throw one report away. They asked how the reports fit together. Al-Bukhari's own chapter heading reads the saying narrowly: it applies, he suggests, when wailing had been the dead person's own custom. Others reconciled it in other ways. And a careful reader asks of any text: does it clash with the Qur'an? With sunnah that's well established? Does it promise a mountain of reward for a tiny act, or speak in a way that doesn't sound like him at all? Later scholars, such as Ibn al-Qayyim, gathered signs like these in their books. The chain gets a report through the door. The text still has to sit at the table with everything else that's known.
screen: `MATN: THE WORDS THEMSELVES.` · `AISHA REACHES FOR THE QUR'AN.` · `HOW DO THE REPORTS FIT?` · `QUESTIONS FOR ANY TEXT.`

segments.voice: Find a quote you've seen lately with a famous name on it: a poster line, a caption, something forwarded with a picture of a scholar or a saint or a president. Set the name aside and look only at the words: does it sound like the rest of what that person said, does it promise too much, does it clash with what they stood for? You don't need a verdict; just ask Aisha's questions, slowly, of one sentence.
Matn. The text of a hadith, what was said or done, tested on its own against the Qur'an and the known sunnah. Today's word.
Your line: the words are tested too. An honest chain can still carry a misheard sentence. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hadith scholars examine a report's text as well as its chain, asking whether it agrees with the Qur'an, with well-established sunnah and with other reports, and they discuss how apparently conflicting reports fit together.

chat.says: If a hadith has honest narrators, isn't it automatically true?
options: Not automatically. Honest people can mishear, so the words are tested too.
Yes. Once the chain is honest, the words never need any checking at all.
Only if a famous companion is in the chain; then the words are certain.
chat.meaning: Aisha said the men who reported it weren't liars, but hearing can slip. So the matn is weighed against the Qur'an and the known sunnah.
